claim: Adolescent growth spurts (GSs) in body length seem to be absent in non-human primates and are considered a distinct human trait.
source: Adolescent growth spurts (GSs) in body length seem to be absent in non-human primates and are considered a distinct human trait.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature in the field.

claim: There is wide consensus that the human adolescent growth spurt (GS) in body length is evolutionary unique and absent in other primates.
source: There is wide consensus that the human adolescent growth spurt (GS) in body length is evolutionary unique and absent in other primates (Bogin, 2020; Gluckman et al., 2013; Hochberg, 2011; Holmgren, 2022; Stevens et al., 2013; Stulp and Barrett, 2016, but see Ellison et al., 2012; Sandel et al., 2023; Watts and Gavan, 1982; Weisfeld, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature, though some dissenting views are also cited.

claim: Adolescent GSs in body weight occur in many primate species, including humans.
source: This is puzzling, because adolescent GSs in body weight occur in many primate species, including humans (Leigh, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leigh, 2001.

claim: The apparent lack of an adolescent length-GS in non-human primates despite often pronounced weight-GSs may largely reflect a methodological problem that results from scaling issues when comparing length- and weight growth rates.
source: However, the apparent lack of an adolescent length-GS in non-human primates despite often pronounced weight-GSs may largely reflect a methodological problem that results from scaling issues when comparing length- and weight growth rates (Cullen et al., 2021; Schmidt-Nielsen, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cullen et al., 2021 and Schmidt-Nielsen, 1984.

claim: The cubic relationship between weight and length growth inevitably results in a decreasing or, at best, constant length growth rate if the acceleration in weight growth rate does not exceed a quadratic function of age.
source: The cubic relationship between weight and length growth inevitably results in a decreasing or, at best, constant length growth rate if the acceleration in weight growth rate does not exceed a quadratic function of age (Figure 1; Cullen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and citation to Cullen et al., 2021, and is based on mathematical scaling relationships.

claim: An acceleration in weight growth rate (=spurt) would be accompanied by a decreasing length growth rate, even if both are perfectly aligned with each other in isometric growth.
source: Hence, in many cases, an acceleration in weight growth rate (=spurt) would be accompanied by a decreasing length growth rate, even if both are perfectly aligned with each other in isometric growth.
evidence: This claim is based on mathematical inference from scaling relationships.

claim: A length-GS is only detectable if the actual acceleration resulting from the weight-GS exceeds the parallel deceleration in length growth rate that results from the cubic relationship.
source: As previously noticed (e.g., Hamada and Udono, 2002), a length-GS is only detectable if the actual acceleration resulting from the weight-GS exceeds the parallel deceleration in length growth rate that results from the cubic relationship.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hamada and Udono, 2002 and is based on mathematical inference.

claim: Whether a linear length-GS is detectable is largely independent of the amplitude of the associated weight-GS.
source: In fact, whether a linear length-GS is detectable is largely independent of the amplitude of the associated weight-GS, and rather depends on various other aspects, such as how fast weight growth rate accelerates, how the level of acceleration changes (e.g., linear or quadratic acceleration), or at which body size the acceleration takes off (for details see Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is based on mathematical inference and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Age trajectories of linear length growth rate are difficult to interpret and require consideration of many aspects.
source: Therefore, age trajectories of linear length growth rate are difficult to interpret and require consideration of many aspects.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the preceding discussion of scaling issues.

claim: A dichotomy between present or absent acceleration in linear length growth seems somewhat arbitrary and leads to misinterpretations.
source: Consequently, a dichotomy between present or absent acceleration in linear length growth seems somewhat arbitrary and leads to misinterpretations (Cullen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cullen et al., 2021 and is based on inference from scaling issues.

claim: Previous findings showed similar peak velocities in weight growth in humans compared to non-human primates during the adolescent GS.
source: Previous findings showed similar peak velocities in weight growth in humans compared to non-human primates during the adolescent GS (Leigh, 2001; Leigh, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Leigh, 2001 and Leigh, 1996.

claim: The resource-limited aspect of growth and thus, the dimension of interest for life history trade-offs is biomass production, and therefore, weight growth.
source: Importantly, the resource-limited aspect of growth and thus, the dimension of interest for life history trade-offs is biomass production, and therefore, weight growth (Leigh, 1996; Schmidt-Nielsen, 1984), which then may also mediate limits on length growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Leigh, 1996 and Schmidt-Nielsen, 1984.

claim: DHEA and DHEA-sulfate (DHEA-S) levels allow to determine the onset of adrenarche, the maturation of the adrenal cortex and the onset of adrenal androgen secretion.
source: First, DHEA and DHEA-sulfate (DHEA-S) levels allow to determine the onset of adrenarche, the maturation of the adrenal cortex and the onset of adrenal androgen secretion.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about DHEA and adrenarche.

claim: Increasing levels of DHEA(-S) might be involved in brain development in apes and humans, and inhibit long-bone growth in humans, paralleling the low growth rates during the juvenile period.
source: Increasing levels of DHEA(-S) might be involved in brain development in apes and humans, and inhibit long-bone growth in humans, paralleling the low growth rates during the juvenile period (Hochberg, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hochberg, 2011 and involves speculative reasoning about DHEA's role.

claim: Changes in testosterone levels indicate testicular maturation in boys and ovarian maturation in girls, and are therefore a physiological marker for the onset of sexual maturation and associated with the adolescence stage in both sexes.
source: Second, changes in testosterone levels indicate testicular maturation in boys and ovarian maturation in girls, and are therefore a physiological marker for the onset of sexual maturation and associated with the adolescence stage in both sexes (Bribiescas, 2010; Muller, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bribiescas, 2010 and Muller, 2017.

claim: Testosterone promotes muscle growth.
source: Furthermore, testosterone promotes muscle growth (Bribiescas, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bribiescas, 2010.

claim: In boys, the adolescent GS in muscle mass lasts longer than the skeletal GS, with muscle growth proceeding into early adulthood.
source: In boys, the adolescent GS in muscle mass lasts longer than the skeletal GS, with muscle growth proceeding into early adulthood (Bogin, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bogin, 2020.

claim: Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) binds to IGFBP-3 for transportation, and levels of both increase with increasing levels of testosterone.
source: Third, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) binds to IGFBP-3 for transportation, and levels of both increase with increasing levels of testosterone.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about IGF-1 and IGFBP-3.

claim: In primates, IGFBP-3 levels increase strongly at the beginning of puberty, and are directly linked to rates of length growth and, in combination with testosterone, to muscle growth during the adolescent GS.
source: Hence in primates, IGFBP-3 levels increase strongly at the beginning of puberty, and are directly linked to rates of length growth and, in combination with testosterone, to muscle growth during the adolescent GS (Bernstein et al., 2008; Juul et al., 1995; Miller, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bernstein et al., 2008, Juul et al., 1995, and Miller, 2022.

claim: In wild-living female bonobos, genital swellings start to increase in size around 5–6 years of age.
source: In wild-living females, genital swellings start to increase in size around 5–6 years of age (Kano, 1992), which is also when female testosterone levels rise in captivity (Behringer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kano, 1992 and Behringer et al., 2014.

claim: Female bonobos disperse from their natal group between 5 and 9 years.
source: Females disperse from their natal group between 5 and 9 years (Toda et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Toda et al., 2022.

claim: In zoo-housed bonobos, menarche occurs between the age of 6 and 11.3 years.
source: In zoo-housed bonobos, menarche occurs between the age of 6 and 11.3 years (Thompson-Handler, 1990; Vervaecke et al., 1999), and they give birth for the first time around 10.7 ± 3.3 years (range: 8–15 years), which is significantly earlier compared to wild populations, where females give first birth around 14.2 years of age (De Lathouwers and Van Elsacker, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thompson-Handler, 1990, Vervaecke et al., 1999, and De Lathouwers and Van Elsacker, 2006.

claim: Zoo-housed female bonobos give birth for the first time around 10.7 ± 3.3 years (range: 8–15 years), which is significantly earlier compared to wild populations, where females give first birth around 14.2 years of age.
source: In zoo-housed bonobos, menarche occurs between the age of 6 and 11.3 years (Thompson-Handler, 1990; Vervaecke et al., 1999), and they give birth for the first time around 10.7 ± 3.3 years (range: 8–15 years), which is significantly earlier compared to wild populations, where females give first birth around 14.2 years of age (De Lathouwers and Van Elsacker, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to De Lathouwers and Van Elsacker, 2006.

claim: In wild male bonobos, testicular descent occurs at 9 years of age.
source: In males, testicular descent occurs at 9 years of age in wild bonobos (Kuroda, 1989) and between the sixth and tenth year of age in captivity (Dahl and Gould, 1997), which corresponds to a fast increase in urinary testosterone levels around the age of 8 years (Behringer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kuroda, 1989.

claim: In captive male bonobos, testicular descent occurs between the sixth and tenth year of age.
source: In males, testicular descent occurs at 9 years of age in wild bonobos (Kuroda, 1989) and between the sixth and tenth year of age in captivity (Dahl and Gould, 1997), which corresponds to a fast increase in urinary testosterone levels around the age of 8 years (Behringer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dahl and Gould, 1997.

claim: Zoo-born male bonobos are on average 12.3 years old at their first reproduction (range 7–17.2 years).
source: Zoo-born males are on average 12.3 years old at their first reproduction (range 7–17.2 years) (Reinartz et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Reinartz et al., 2002.

claim: Zoo-housed female bonobos outlive males by several decades.
source: Zoo-housed females outlive males by several decades (Stevens, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stevens, 2020.

claim: Compared to other hominoid primates, sexual dimorphism in adult body weight is exceptionally small in bonobos.
source: Compared to other hominoid primates, sexual dimorphism in adult body weight is exceptionally small in bonobos (Leigh and Shea, 1995), and preliminary data on linear dimensions such as postcranial skeleton, body segments, and forearm length suggest a complete absence of sexual size dimorphism in body length (Behringer et al., 2016a; Druelle et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leigh and Shea, 1995.

claim: Preliminary data on linear dimensions such as postcranial skeleton, body segments, and forearm length suggest a complete absence of sexual size dimorphism in body length in bonobos.
source: Compared to other hominoid primates, sexual dimorphism in adult body weight is exceptionally small in bonobos (Leigh and Shea, 1995), and preliminary data on linear dimensions such as postcranial skeleton, body segments, and forearm length suggest a complete absence of sexual size dimorphism in body length (Behringer et al., 2016a; Druelle et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Behringer et al., 2016a and Druelle et al., 2018.

claim: Based on 13 males and 23 females, it was suggested that both male and female bonobos experience a subadult GS in body weight.
source: For example, based on 13 males and 23 females, it was suggested that both male and female bonobos experience a subadult GS in body weight (Leigh, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leigh, 1996.

claim: Both male and female bonobos showed a pronounced GS in body weight.
source: Both males and females showed a pronounced GS in body weight (Figure 2A) that was accompanied by a similarly pronounced GS in forearm length which almost perfectly aligned in timing and amplitude (Figure 2B and 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 2A, 2B, and 4A.

claim: The GS in body weight was accompanied by a similarly pronounced GS in forearm length which almost perfectly aligned in timing and amplitude.
source: Both males and females showed a pronounced GS in body weight (Figure 2A) that was accompanied by a similarly pronounced GS in forearm length which almost perfectly aligned in timing and amplitude (Figure 2B and 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 2A, 2B, and 4A.

claim: Compared to females, male bonobos reached peak growth velocity in both body weight and forearm length 2 years later (6 vs. 8 years of age).
source: Compared to females, male bonobos reached peak growth velocity in both body weight and forearm length 2 years later (6 vs. 8 years of age), and had a longer and in case of weight growth also more pronounced GS, which resulted in a larger adult body size in males (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Male bonobos had a longer and in case of weight growth also more pronounced GS, which resulted in a larger adult body size in males.
source: Compared to females, male bonobos reached peak growth velocity in both body weight and forearm length 2 years later (6 vs. 8 years of age), and had a longer and in case of weight growth also more pronounced GS, which resulted in a larger adult body size in males (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: There was no period of decelerated growth prior to the GS in either sex of bonobos.
source: There was no period of decelerated growth prior to this GS in either sex.
evidence: This claim is based on the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: The pronounced GS in male forearm length was only evident if analysed at the weight dimension (i.e., raised to the power of cm2.5).
source: The pronounced GS in male forearm length was only evident if analysed at the weight dimension (i.e., raised to the power of cm2.5, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The GS in female forearm length was also evident if investigated at linear length (in cm/year).
source: Remarkably though, the GS in female forearm length was also evident if investigated at linear length (in cm/year, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Female length growth reached its peak velocity about 1 year earlier when reported in cm/year compared to cm2.5/year.
source: However, female length growth reached its peak velocity about 1 year earlier when reported in cm/year compared to cm2.5/year (Figure 4A, red and blue dotted line), as predicted based on the mathematical scaling relationship (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 4A and 1.

claim: Only the corrected GS (in cm2.5/year) matched the GS in body weight.
source: Consequently, only the corrected GS (in cm2.5/year) matched the GS in body weight (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: If down-scaling body weight to the dimension of linear length growth (i.e., extracting the 2.5th root), the pronounced weight-GSs were no longer detectable, and the resulting pattern matched the trajectories in linear length growth (in cm).
source: Reversely, if down-scaling body weight to the dimension of linear length growth (i.e., extracting the 2.5th root, Figure 2C), the pronounced weight-GSs were no longer detectable, and the resulting pattern matched the trajectories in linear length growth (in cm, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Male bonobos showed a GS in lean body respective muscle mass.
source: We also found a GS in lean body respective muscle mass in males (Figure 3A), which was 1.5 years after the length- and the weight-GS (Figure 4A), though the difference in timing was within the 95% CIs and not significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 3A and 4A.

claim: The GS in lean body mass in males was 1.5 years after the length- and the weight-GS, though the difference in timing was within the 95% CIs and not significant.
source: We also found a GS in lean body respective muscle mass in males (Figure 3A), which was 1.5 years after the length- and the weight-GS (Figure 4A), though the difference in timing was within the 95% CIs and not significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 3A and 4A.

claim: In female bonobos, there was no particular peak in the lean body mass growth rate, but growth rate was highest until 5 years of age and decreased thereafter.
source: In females, we found no particular peak in the lean body mass growth rate, but growth rate was highest until 5 years of age and decreased thereafter (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Growth patterns and DHEA levels were not associated in bonobos.
source: As predicted for an adolescent GS, growth patterns and DHEA levels were not associated, and DHEA levels did not show any sex difference in levels or age trajectories that would align to the sex differences in growth (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: DHEA levels did not show any sex difference in levels or age trajectories that would align to the sex differences in growth in bonobos.
source: As predicted for an adolescent GS, growth patterns and DHEA levels were not associated, and DHEA levels did not show any sex difference in levels or age trajectories that would align to the sex differences in growth (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: In both males and females bonobos, testosterone and IGFBP-3 levels increased largely together but in a sex-specific manner, rising at an earlier age in females than males.
source: In both males and females, testosterone and IGFBP-3 levels increased largely together (within the wide range of 95% CIs particularly for IGFBP-3) but in a sex-specific manner, rising at an earlier age in females than males (Figures 3C, D, 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 3C, 3D, and 4B.

claim: IGFBP-3 levels reached similar maximal levels in both sexes of bonobos and declined thereafter.
source: IGFBP-3 levels reached similar maximal levels in both sexes and declined thereafter (Figure 3D), whereas testosterone levels increased for longer and reached higher levels in males than females, and remained at the maximum level for many years (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Testosterone levels increased for longer and reached higher levels in males than females bonobos, and remained at the maximum level for many years.
source: IGFBP-3 levels reached similar maximal levels in both sexes and declined thereafter (Figure 3D), whereas testosterone levels increased for longer and reached higher levels in males than females, and remained at the maximum level for many years (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Testosterone levels increased fast at the age of GS take-off in both sexes of bonobos.
source: Testosterone levels increased fast at the age of GS take-off in both sexes (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: In female bonobos, testosterone reached maximum levels already before the age of peak growth velocity.
source: Testosterone reached maximum levels already before the age of peak growth velocity in females, but slightly after the peak in length- and weight-growth and more closely to the peak in muscle-growth in males.
evidence: This claim is based on the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: In male bonobos, testosterone reached maximum levels slightly after the peak in length- and weight-growth and more closely to the peak in muscle-growth.
source: Testosterone reached maximum levels already before the age of peak growth velocity in females, but slightly after the peak in length- and weight-growth and more closely to the peak in muscle-growth in males.
evidence: This claim is based on the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: The weight- and length-GSs were largely aligned with IGFBP-3 levels in bonobos.
source: The weight- and length-GSs were largely aligned with IGFBP-3 levels (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: In female bonobos, IGFBP-3 levels directly aligned with the GS in length and weight and peaked at the same age.
source: In females, IGFBP-3 levels directly aligned with the GS in length and weight and peaked at the same age, whereas in males they reached their maximum levels after the peak in weight and length growth and better matched changes in muscle growth rates, also after considering the wide range of 95% CIs for IGFBP-3.
evidence: This claim is based on the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: In male bonobos, IGFBP-3 levels reached their maximum levels after the peak in weight and length growth and better matched changes in muscle growth rates.
source: In females, IGFBP-3 levels directly aligned with the GS in length and weight and peaked at the same age, whereas in males they reached their maximum levels after the peak in weight and length growth and better matched changes in muscle growth rates, also after considering the wide range of 95% CIs for IGFBP-3.
evidence: This claim is based on the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: DHEA and testosterone levels declined after 30 years of age in bonobos.
source: DHEA and testosterone levels declined after 30 years of age (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: For nine primate species, there was evidence for an acceleration in linear length growth in at least one sex.
source: For nine species, there was evidence for an acceleration in linear length growth in at least one sex, with all other species showing a period of constant length growth rate or a slowdown in the deceleration.
evidence: This claim is based on literature review presented in Table 2.

claim: In wild Assamese macaques, linear length growth rate only showed a slowdown in deceleration whereas cubic-transformed values showed a significant acceleration in length growth, which occurred also at a later age then the slowdown in linear length growth.
source: In wild Assamese macaques (Macaca assamensis), linear length growth rate only showed a slowdown in deceleration whereas cubic-transformed values showed a significant acceleration in length growth, which occurred also at a later age then the slowdown in linear length growth.
evidence: This claim is based on literature review and reanalysis of published data.

claim: In Pigtailed macaques, cubic-root-transformed weight measures were perfectly linearly correlated with length values.
source: In Pigtailed macaques (Macaca nemestrina), cubic-root-transformed weight measures were perfectly linearly correlated with length values.
evidence: This claim is based on literature review and reanalysis of published data.

claim: For 10 primate species for which parallel weight growth data were available, the respective pattern in linear length coincided with a weight-GS, but this linear pattern appeared at younger ages than the weight-GS in all species where available data allowed for such detailed analyses.
source: For 10 species for which parallel weight growth data were available, the respective pattern in linear length coincided with a weight-GS, but as predicted, this linear pattern appeared at younger ages than the weight-GS in all species where available data allowed for such detailed analyses.
evidence: This claim is based on literature review presented in Table 2.

claim: GSs in primates occurred at similar ages as reported markers of adolescence within a species.
source: Overall, GSs occurred at similar ages as reported markers of adolescence within a species, but this comparison was often coarse and non-conclusive, as e.g., age at menarche or first cycling was highly variable for females of most ape species, and increase in male testes size and testosterone levels were often aligned with, but sometimes also occurred at later ages than the GSs (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on literature review presented in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: The bonobo results on weight growth and adult sex difference in body weight largely match previous results.
source: Our results on weight growth and adult sex difference in body weight largely match previous results (Leigh, 1996), but peak velocity occurred 1 year later in both sexes in our study, indicating a stronger and more human-like delay of the adolescent GS than previously assumed (Leigh, 2001; Leigh, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with citations to Leigh, 1996.

claim: Peak velocity in bonobo weight growth occurred 1 year later in both sexes in this study compared to previous results, indicating a stronger and more human-like delay of the adolescent GS than previously assumed.
source: Our results on weight growth and adult sex difference in body weight largely match previous results (Leigh, 1996), but peak velocity occurred 1 year later in both sexes in our study, indicating a stronger and more human-like delay of the adolescent GS than previously assumed (Leigh, 2001; Leigh, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with citations to Leigh, 2001 and Leigh, 1996, and data from the study.

claim: In contrast to previous results on much smaller sample sizes, this study found an adult sex difference in forearm length in bonobos, indicating a sexual size dimorphism in length.
source: In contrast to previous results on much smaller sample sizes (Behringer et al., 2016a; Druelle et al., 2018) we also found an adult sex difference in forearm length, indicating a sexual size dimorphism in length in bonobos.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with citations to Behringer et al., 2016a and Druelle et al., 2018, and data from the study.

claim: Creatinine measurement can show high uncertainty before the age of 3 years.
source: However, a muscle GS in females may have been masked because creatinine measurement can show high uncertainty before the age of 3 years (Emery Thompson et al., 2012), hence our result on sex-specific muscle growth in bonobos should be interpreted with caution and needs further validation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Emery Thompson et al., 2012.

claim: The results on testosterone trajectories in bonobos confirm the previous finding that testosterone levels reach maximal values at a much younger age in female bonobos compared to male bonobos.
source: Our results on testosterone trajectories confirm the previous finding that testosterone levels reach maximal values at a much younger age in female bonobos compared to male bonobos (Behringer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Behringer et al., 2014 and data from the study.

claim: In female bonobos, testosterone levels showed a fast rise at about 4 years of age and reached maximal levels at 5 years of age.
source: In females, testosterone levels showed a fast rise at about 4 years of age and reached maximal levels at 5 years of age, matching previous results on testosterone level changes (Behringer et al., 2014), menarche at 6–11 years of age in zoo-housed females (Thompson-Handler, 1990; Vervaecke et al., 1999), and increasing external genitalia with 5–6 years of age in wild female bonobos (Kano, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and citations to Behringer et al., 2014, Thompson-Handler, 1990, Vervaecke et al., 1999, and Kano, 1992.

claim: In male bonobos, testosterone levels showed a fast increase at about 7 years of age and reached maximal levels at about 9 years of age.
source: In males, testosterone levels showed a fast increase at about 7 years of age and reached maximal levels at about 9 years of age, which is in line with previous results on testosterone level changes (Behringer et al., 2014), testicular descent at 9 years of age in wild (Kuroda, 1989), and between 6 and 10 years of age in zoo-housed male bonobos (Dahl and Gould, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and citations to Behringer et al., 2014, Kuroda, 1989, and Dahl and Gould, 1997.

claim: The GSs found in bonobos mirror human adolescence patterns and therefore represent adolescent GSs.
source: In any case, our results suggest that the GSs found in our study in bonobos mirror human adolescence patterns (Bogin, 2020), and therefore, represent adolescent GSs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and comparison with citation to Bogin, 2020.

claim: The results on bonobos provide proof that at least some bonobo populations show pronounced adolescent length-GSs, which challenge the hypothesis that an adolescent length-GS is a unique human trait.
source: However, this affects our main conclusion only marginally, as our results still provide proof that at least some bonobo populations show pronounced adolescent length-GSs, which challenge the hypothesis that an adolescent length-GS is a unique human trait.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data presented in the study.

claim: A recent study provides initial evidence of an adolescent bone GS in wild-living chimpanzees.
source: In addition, our findings have been corroborated by a recent study, which provides initial evidence of an adolescent bone GS in wild-living chimpanzees (Sandel et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sandel et al., 2023.

claim: The human adolescent length-GS is also evident on the linear scale and more pronounced than in any other primate, including bonobos.
source: Indeed, the human adolescent length-GS is also evident on the linear scale and more pronounced than in any other primate, including our results on bonobos.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the study's data with established knowledge about human growth.

claim: Human body length growth rates during the GS are almost identical with those in chimpanzees, with average peak velocity of height growth in humans being 9–11 cm/year for boys and 7–9 cm/year for girls, and in chimpanzees 8–10 cm/year in males and 6–10 cm/year in females.
source: However, human body length growth rates during the GS are almost identical with those in chimpanzees, with average peak velocity of height growth in humans being 9–11 cm/year for boys and 7–9 cm/year for girls, and in chimpanzees 8–10 cm/year in males and 6–10 cm/year in females (Bogin, 2020; Hamada and Udono, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bogin, 2020 and Hamada and Udono, 2002.

claim: The length growth rates of the forearms in bonobos match or even exceed human forearm growth rates during the adolescent GS.
source: Similarly, also the length growth rates of the forearms in our study match or even exceed human forearm growth rates during the adolescent GS (Nowak-Szczepanska and Koziel, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the study's data with citation to Nowak-Szczepanska and Koziel, 2016.

claim: Human-like length growth rates were also found in captive Japanese macaques, despite their smaller body size.
source: Human-like length growth rates were also found in e.g. captive Japanese macaques, despite their smaller body size (Hamada et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hamada et al., 1999.

claim: Humans show a juvenile period of particularly slow weight growth from which the adolescent GS has to rise, which seems absent in non-human primates including bonobos.
source: First, humans show a juvenile period of particularly slow weight growth from which the adolescent GS has to rise, which seems absent in non-human primates including our results on bonobos (Bogin, 2020; Leigh, 1996; Watts and Gavan, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bogin, 2020, Leigh, 1996, and Watts and Gavan, 1982, and data from the study.

claim: The human adolescent GS is squeezed, taking less time relative to body size than in other primates.
source: Second, the human adolescent GS is squeezed, taking less time relative to body size than in other primates (Leigh, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leigh, 2001.

claim: Humans and chimpanzees as well as bonobos have a delayed onset of the adolescent weight-GS compared to other primates.
source: Additionally, the detectability and magnitude of a length-GS increases with the body weight at which the acceleration in weight growth takes off. Here, humans and chimpanzees as well as bonobos have a delayed onset of the adolescent weight-GS compared to other primates (Leigh, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leigh, 2001.

claim: Humans seem to accomplish the same proportion of their adult body weight during the GS as other primates do.
source: Finally, although humans seem to accomplish the same proportion of their adult body weight during the GS as other primates do (Leigh, 2001), they accomplish a larger proportion of their adult body length during the GS than at least chimpanzees do (Smith, 1993), which could cause a higher detectability on its own and may indicate some differences in allometry between humans and chimpanzees.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leigh, 2001.

claim: Humans accomplish a larger proportion of their adult body length during the GS than at least chimpanzees do, which could cause a higher detectability on its own and may indicate some differences in allometry between humans and chimpanzees.
source: Finally, although humans seem to accomplish the same proportion of their adult body weight during the GS as other primates do (Leigh, 2001), they accomplish a larger proportion of their adult body length during the GS than at least chimpanzees do (Smith, 1993), which could cause a higher detectability on its own and may indicate some differences in allometry between humans and chimpanzees.

claim: Length-GSs might be more widespread and pronounced in primates than previously thought, and might align with weight-GSs and, in some species, with certain indicators of adolescence.
source: Our primate literature search on available length growth data showed that length-GSs might be more widespread and pronounced in primates than previously thought, and might align with weight-GSs and, in some species, with certain indicators of adolescence.
evidence: This claim is based on literature review and inference.

claim: Analyses of linear length growth very likely underestimate the magnitude and age of length-GSs, and thus their alignment with weight growth.
source: However, these studies would still benefit from a reanalysis of scale-corrected data, since analyses of linear length growth very likely underestimate the magnitude and age of these length-GSs, and thus their alignment with weight growth.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the scaling issues discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Aligning length-GSs can be expected in species that show constant growth rates in linear length during their weight-GSs, like in both sexes of mandrils, or in male baboons and female geladas.
source: Aligning length-GSs can further be expected in species that show constant growth rates in linear length during their weight-GSs (Figure 1C), like in both sexes of mandrils, or in male baboons (Papio hamadryas) and female geladas (Theropithecus gelada) (Leigh, 2009; Lu et al., 2016; Setchell et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from Figure 1C and citations to Leigh, 2009, Lu et al., 2016, and Setchell et al., 2001.

claim: In non-human primates, weight-GSs and length growth are not decoupled and in 'sharp contrast' but rather aligned with each other, and the apparent absence of length-GSs despite in parts pronounced weight-GS is merely a mathematical artefact.
source: These patterns indicate that in non-human primates, weight-GSs and length growth are not decoupled and in 'sharp contrast' (Bogin, 2020, p. 180) but rather aligned with each other, and the apparent absence of length-GSs despite in parts pronounced weight-GS is merely a mathematical artefact.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and literature review, and challenges citation to Bogin, 2020.

claim: Previous findings that in humans and other primates, length-GSs do not align with but precede weight-GSs could be an artefact of comparing weight and length growth rate at different dimensions.
source: This may for example apply to previous findings that in humans and other primates, length-GSs do not align with but precede weight-GSs (Hamada et al., 1999; Leigh, 2009; Tanner et al., 1990). Again, this could be an artefact of comparing weight and length growth rate at different dimensions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from scaling issues and citations to Hamada et al., 1999, Leigh, 2009, and Tanner et al., 1990.

claim: Even if a linear length-GS is detectable, it will by definition reach its peak velocity at an earlier age than the associated weight-GS since linear growth starts to decline already when weight (and exponentiated length) growth rate is still rising, resulting in an artificial time lag even if the weight and length-GSs are perfectly synchronous.
source: Even if a linear length-GS is detectable, it will by definition reach its peak velocity at an earlier age than the associated weight-GS since linear growth starts to decline already when weight (and exponentiated length) growth rate is still rising (Figure 1F), resulting in an artificial time lag even if the weight and length-GSs are perfectly synchronous.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from Figure 1F and mathematical scaling relationships.

claim: The time lag seen in humans and other primates between length and weight GSs may be a mathematical artefact.
source: Hence, the time lag seen in humans and other primates may be a mathematical artefact, altogether.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and scaling issues discussed.

claim: If compared at comparable scales, the adolescent GSs in bonobos, and probably primate GSs in general, encompass similar changes in weight and length growth rates which correspond well with each other.
source: Altogether, our results show that if compared at comparable scales, the adolescent GSs in bonobos, and probably primate GSs in general, encompass similar changes in weight and length growth rates which correspond well with each other.
evidence: This claim is based on the data from the study and inference to other primates.

claim: The proposed general uniqueness of the human adolescent GS in length growth can be rebutted.
